lines: - Since Spark 4.4, when `spark.sql.parquet.fieldId.read.enabled` is true, a Parquet read fails with `PARQUET_FIELD_REQUESTED_MORE_THAN_ONCE` if two or more requested fields of a struct (or of the top-level schema) resolve to the same Parquet field. This happens when one requested field is matched by field ID and another by name, or when two requested fields have the same field ID. In Spark 4.3 and earlier, such a read returned wrong values without an error: with the vectorized reader one of the fields read as non-null default values (for example `0`) or uninitialized data, and with the parquet-mr reader (`spark.sql.parquet.enableVectorizedReader` set to `false`) one of the fields read as `null`. To read the Parquet field more than once, request it once and refer to the resulting column more than once in the query.

- Since Spark 4.4, when `spark.sql.groupByOrdinal` is true (the default), the pipe `AGGREGATE` operator rejects an aliased integer literal in its `GROUP BY` clause, such as `TABLE t |> AGGREGATE sum(x) AS s GROUP BY 2 AS grp`, with `UNSUPPORTED_FEATURE.PIPE_OPERATOR_AGGREGATE_UNSUPPORTED_CASE`, because a bare integer literal in the same position is an ordinal. Previously the aliased literal was grouped as a constant. Bare ordinals and aliases on other grouping expressions are not affected. To restore the previous behavior, set `spark.sql.legacy.allowAliasedPipeAggregateOrdinals` to `true`.

- Since Spark 4.4, with whole-stage codegen enabled, a filter condition, including the `FILTER` clause of an aggregate function, evaluates the remaining top-level conjuncts of the condition on a row after one of them evaluates to `NULL`, as the SQL standard requires, and does so in the order they appear in the condition, as Spark already did with whole-stage codegen disabled, which also evaluates a subexpression shared by several conjuncts before the condition. Only a `FALSE` conjunct stops the evaluation. One exception: an `IS NOT NULL` check on a column, or on an expression over it, that a later conjunct references is still evaluated before that conjunct and the conjuncts up to the check's own position, even when it is written after them, and can drop the row before an error one of them raises. Once a condition has a conjunct that can be `NULL`, the `IS NOT NULL` checks after that conjunct are evaluated in the order of the condition on every row, not only on rows where a conjunct is `NULL`. A row whose condition is `NULL` is still dropped, but an error raised by a later conjunct on that row, such as `ARITHMETIC_OVERFLOW` in ANSI mode, now fails the query. For example, `SELECT a FROM t WHERE NOT (a > 0 AND b > 0) AND y + 1 > 0` can fail with `ARITHMETIC_OVERFLOW` on a row where `a` is `NULL`, `b` is `1`, and `y` is `2147483647`, unless the row is dropped earlier by a `FALSE` conjunct or `IS NOT NULL` check that precedes `y + 1 > 0` in the condition, or skipped before the filter, for example by data source filter pushdown such as Parquet row group statistics. Previously the query skipped such a row with whole-stage codegen enabled. The later conjuncts also run on more rows than before, so a nondeterministic conjunct such as `rand(seed)` can return different values on the remaining rows, and a side-effecting user-defined function is called on rows that are dropped. To restore the previous behavior, set `spark.sql.legacy.filterShortCircuitOnNullConjunct` to `true`.

-- Since Spark 4.4, the optimizer no longer infers a filter from data constraints when evaluating the filter can fail, such as arithmetic or a narrowing cast in ANSI mode, or when it calls a user-defined function. The check is conservative, so a few filters that cannot fail are not inferred either, such as `LIKE 'a%'`, `year(d) = 2024`, and arithmetic with ANSI mode off. For example, `SELECT * FROM t WHERE x = y AND 10 / y > 0` no longer adds the filter `10 / x > 0`, which failed with `DIVIDE_BY_ZERO` on a row where `x` is `0` and `y` is `6`, although the query itself never divides by `x`. As a result, such a query no longer fails, a user-defined function is no longer evaluated twice per row, and such a filter no longer reaches the other side of a join, a data source, or partition pruning, so the query can read more data. Filters on plain comparisons, `IN`, `BETWEEN`, widening numeric casts, integral remainders by a non-zero constant such as `x % 2 = 0`, constants, and subqueries whose correlation condition cannot fail are still inferred. To restore the previous behavior, set `spark.sql.legacy.inferFailableFiltersFromConstraints` to `true`.

+- Since Spark 4.4, the optimizer no longer infers a filter from data constraints when evaluating the filter can fail, such as, in ANSI mode, integral or decimal arithmetic, a division or a narrowing cast, or when it calls a user-defined function. The check is conservative, so a few filters that cannot fail are not inferred either, such as `upper(s) = 'A'`. For example, with ANSI mode on, `SELECT * FROM t WHERE x = y AND 10 / y > 0` no longer adds the filter `10 / x > 0`, which failed with `DIVIDE_BY_ZERO` on a row where `x` is `0` and `y` is `6`, although the query itself never divides by `x`. As a result, such a query no longer fails, a user-defined function is no longer evaluated twice per row, and such a filter no longer reaches the other side of a join, a data source, or partition pruning, so the query can read more data. Filters on plain comparisons, `IN`, `BETWEEN`, widening numeric casts, integral remainders by a non-zero constant such as `x % 2 = 0`, constants, subqueries whose correlation condition cannot fail, and many other expressions that cannot fail, such as `LIKE 'a%'`, `year(d) = 2024`, numeric arithmetic with ANSI mode off, and `+`, `-` and `*` over `FLOAT` and `DOUBLE` in any mode, are still inferred. To restore the previous behavior, set `spark.sql.legacy.inferFailableFiltersFromConstraints` to `true`.

- Since Spark 4.4, when a format is specified, `to_timestamp`, `try_to_timestamp`, and `to_timestamp_ltz` cast a numeric first argument to a string and parse it with the format, for example `to_timestamp(20201231, 'yyyyMMdd')` returns `2020-12-31 00:00:00`. This matches the existing behavior when `spark.sql.timestampType` is `TIMESTAMP_NTZ`. Previously, with the default `TIMESTAMP_LTZ` timestamp type, such calls failed with `INTERNAL_ERROR`. Note that the string form of the number is parsed, so a DECIMAL `1.5` is parsed as `"1.5"`.

- Since Spark 4.4, the Spark Thrift Server logs a warning at startup when `hive.server2.enable.doAs` is `true` and `hive.server2.authentication` verifies user identities (any recognized type other than `NONE`/`NOSASL`), because executor-side data access still runs as the server's own service identity rather than the connecting user (SPARK-5159). Set `spark.sql.hive.thriftServer.allowIneffectiveDoAs` to `true` to acknowledge the limitation and silence the warning. Spark 5.0 is expected to refuse to start on this configuration unless that option is set.

- Since Spark 4.4, `UPDATE` and `MERGE` on a Data Source V2 table fail with `DATATYPE_MISMATCH.INVALID_ROW_LEVEL_OPERATION_ASSIGNMENTS` when they assign to a metadata column of the table. This includes `UPDATE SET *` and `INSERT *` in `MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION` when the source has a column with the name of a metadata column of the target table. Previously, these assignments passed analysis and were usually ignored. To restore the previous behavior, set `spark.sql.legacy.ignoreMetadataColumnAssignments` to `true`.
